{{Short description|Theorem in geometry}}
[[File:Tetrahedron centroid gimp.png|thumb|upright=1.5|Medians of a tetrahedron intersecting in a point <math>S</math> (its centroid), such that<br/><math>\frac{|AS|}{|SS_{BCD}|}=\frac{|BS|}{|SS_{ACD}|}=\frac{|CS|}{|SS_{ABD}|}=\frac{|DS|}{|SS_{ABC}|}=\frac{3}{1}</math>]]
'''Commandino's theorem''', named after [[Federico Commandino]] (1509–1575), states that the four [[Median (geometry)|median]]s of a [[tetrahedron]] are concurrent at a point ''S'', which divides them in a 3:1 ratio. In a tetrahedron a median is a line segment that connects a vertex with the [[centroid]] of the opposite [[Face (geometry)|face]] – that is, the centroid of the opposite triangle. The point ''S'' is also the centroid of the tetrahedron.<ref>Claudi Alsina, Roger B. Nelsen: ''A Mathematical Space Odyssey: Solid Geometry in the 21st Century''. The Mathematical Association of America, 2015, {{ISBN|9780883853580}}, pp. 97–98</ref><ref>Nathan Altshiller-Court: ''The Tetrahedron and Its Circumscribed Parallelepiped''. The Mathematics Teacher, Vol. 26, No. 1 (JANUARY 1933), pp. 46–52 ([https://www.jstor.org/stable/27951513 JSTOR])</ref><ref>Norman Schaumberger: ''Commandino's theorem''. The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal, Vol. 13, No. 5 (Nov., 1982), p. 331 ([https://www.jstor.org/stable/3026506 JSTOR])</ref>

== History ==
The theorem is attributed to Commandino, who stated, in his work ''De Centro Gravitatis Solidorum'' (The Center of Gravity of Solids, 1565), that the four medians of the tetrahedron are concurrent. However, according to the 19th century scholar Guillaume Libri, [[Francesco Maurolico]] (1494–1575) claimed to have found the result earlier. Libri nevertheless thought that it had been known even earlier to [[Leonardo da Vinci]], who seemed to have used it in his work. [[Julian Coolidge]] shared that assessment but pointed out that he couldn't find any explicit description or mathematical treatment of the theorem in da Vinci's works.<ref>Nathan Altshiller Court: ''Notes on the centroid''. The Mathematics Teacher, Vol. 53, No. 1 (JANUARY 1960), pp. 34 ([https://www.jstor.org/stable/27956057 JSTOR])</ref> Other scholars have speculated that the result may have already been known to Greek mathematicians during antiquity.<ref>Howard Eves: ''Great Moments in Mathematics (before 1650)''. MAA, 1983, {{ISBN|9780883853108}}, p. 225</ref>

==Generalizations==
Commandino's theorem has a direct analog for [[simplex]]es of any [[dimension]]:<ref>{{Cite book|author=[[Egbert Harzheim]]|title=Einführung in die kombinatorische Topologie|date=1978|publisher=Wissenschaftliche Buchgesellschaft|ISBN=3-534-07016-X|place=Darmstadt|pages=33|language=de}}</ref>

: Let <math> \Delta </math> be a <math>d</math>-simplex of some dimension <math>d>1</math> in <math>\R^n \; (d,n \in \N , n \geq d) </math> and let <math>V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_p</math> be its vertices. Furthermore, let <math> \ell_0, \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d</math>, be the medians of <math> \Delta </math>, the lines joining each vertex <math>V_i</math> with the centroid of the opposite <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional [[facet (geometry)|facet]] <math>V_0\ldots V_{i-1}V_{i+1}\ldots V_d</math>. Then, these lines intersect each other in a point <math>S</math>, in a ratio of <math>d:1</math>.

=== Full generality ===
The former analog is easy to prove via the following, more general result, which is analogous to the way [[Lever|levers]] in physics work:<ref>{{citation|surname1=[[Egbert Harzheim]]|title=Einführung in die Kombinatorische Topologie|publication-place=Darmstadt|at=p.&nbsp;31|isbn=3-534-07016-X|date=1978|language=de
}}</ref>

: Let <math>m</math> and <math>k</math> be [[Natural number|natural numbers]], so that in an <math>\R</math>-[[vector space]] <math>\mathcal {V}</math>, <math>m+k</math> pairwise different [[Point (geometry)|points]] <math>X_1, \dots, X_m, Y_1, \dots, Y_k \in \mathcal {V} </math> are given.
: Let <math>S_X</math> be the centroid of the points <math>X_i \; (i=1, \dots, m)</math>, let <math>S_Y</math> be the centroid of the points <math>Y_j \; (j=1, \dots, k)</math>, and let <math>S</math> be the centroid of all of these <math>m+k</math> points.
: Then, one has
::<math>S = S_X + \frac{k}{m+k} (S_Y-S_X)  = \frac{m}{m+k} S_X + \frac{k}{m+k} S_Y.
</math>
: In particular, the centroid <math>S</math> lies on the line <math>\overline{ {S_X} {S_Y}}</math> and divides it in a ratio of <math>k:m</math>.

=== Reusch's theorem ===
The previous theorem has further interesting consequences other than the aforementioned generalization of Commandino's theorem. It can be used to prove the following theorem about the centroid of a tetrahedron, first described in the ''Mathematische Unterhaltungen'' by the German [[physicist]] {{ill|Friedrich Eduard Reusch|de|Friedrich Eduard Reusch}}:<ref name="FJPR_I">Friedrich Joseph Pythagoras Riecke (Hrsg.): ''Mathematische Unterhaltungen. Zweites Heft.'' 1973, S. 100, 128</ref><ref>In den ''Mathematische Unterhaltungen'' (Zweites Heft, S. 128) wird auf die S. 36 von Reuschs Abhandlung [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.fl33pn;view=1up;seq=7 ''Der Spitzbogen''] verwiesen.</ref>
{{blockquote|One may find the centroid of a tetrahedron by taking the [[Midpoint|midpoints]] of two pairs of two of its opposite [[Edge (geometry)|edges]] and connecting the corresponding midpoints through their respective midline. The intersection point of both midlines will be the centroid of the tetrahedron.}}

Since a tetrahedron has six edges in three opposite pairs, one obtains the following corollary:<ref name="FJPR_I" />
{{blockquote|In a tetrahedron, the three midlines corresponding to opposite edge midpoints are [[Concurrent lines|concurrent]], and their intersection point is the centroid of the tetrahedron.}}

=== Varignon's theorem ===
A specific case of Reusch's theorem where all four vertices of a tetrahedron are [[Coplanarity|coplanar]] and lie on a single plane, thereby degenerating into a [[quadrilateral]], Varignon's theorem, named after [[Pierre Varignon]], states the following:<ref name="HSMC_I">Coxeter, op. cit., S. 242</ref><ref name="DUDEN">''DUDEN: Rechnen und Mathematik.'' 1985, S. 652</ref>
{{blockquote|Let a quadrilateral in <math>\R^2 </math> be given. Then the two midlines connecting opposite edge midpoints intersect in the centroid of the quadrilateral and are divided in half by it.}}
